pages.title: MCQ - Permutation Subsequence Calculation
pages.content:
Let's say a number $x$ appears $f[x]$ times in the array $A$. \
In how many ways can you form a permutation subsequence of size $L$?

Option 1: $\prod_{i=1}^L (f[i] + 1)$ 

We are increasing the frequency of each element by 1 and then multiplying it with the frequencies of the other elements, which are also increased by 1.

Option 2: $\prod_{i=1}^L f[i]$ 

We are taking the frequency of each element and then multiplying it with the frequencies of the other elements.

Option 3: $1 + \prod_{i=1}^L f[i]$ 

We are taking the frequency of each element, multiplying it with the frequencies of the other elements, and adding 1 at last.

Option 4: $\sum_{i=1}^L f[i]$ 

We are adding the frequency of all the element.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: MCQ - Permutation Subsequence Calculation focuses on a specific combinatorics technique. Identify the counting model before implementing it.

pages.title: Concept - Optimizing Permutation Calculation
pages.content:
So now we need to simply find number of ways we can form all the permutation from size $1$ to $N$.

This is equal to 
$$
\sum_{L = 1}^N (\prod_{i = 1}^L f[i])
$$

To optimize it, note that that we’re essentially taking prefix products of the $\text{f}$ array, and all of those can be computed in $\mathcal{O}(N)$ time total once $\text{f}$ is known, thus solving the problem in $\mathcal{O}(N)$.

pages.title: MCQ - Stone Color Patterns
pages.content:
Which of the following will hold true?
1. For $i > K$, stone $i$ will have same colour as stone $i - K$.
2. If paints of all the stones from $1$ to $i - 1$ are fixed, then $i$-th stone can be painted in $K$ ways
3. For $i > K$, stone $i$ will have same colour as stone $i - 2 \cdot K$.
4. None of these.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: MCQ - Stone Color Patterns focuses on a specific combinatorics technique. Identify the counting model before implementing it.

pages.title: Concept - Coloring Stones Combinations
pages.content:
Let’s try to color the stones one at a time, from $1$ to $N$.

- Stone $1$ can be colored in any of the $K$ colors, there are no restrictions yet.
- Stone $2$ has $K-1$ options, since it can’t be the same color as $1$.
- Stone $3$ has $K-2$ options, it can’t be the same color as the previous two.
- $\vdots$
- Stone $K-1$ has $2$ options.
- Stone $K$ has $1$ option, since it can’t be any of the previous $K-1$ colors (which are all distinct).
- Stone $K+1$ has only one option: it can’t take the color of any of stones $2, 3, \ldots, K$; but it can take the color of stone $1$.
- Similarly, stone $K+2$ must have the same color as stone $2$, and so on.

In general, if $i \gt K$ then stone $i$ will have exactly one option: have the same color as stone $i-K$.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Concept - Coloring Stones Combinations focuses on a specific combinatorics technique. Identify the counting model before implementing it.

pages.title: Concept -  Stone Painting Choices
pages.content:
If $K \leq N$, answer will be $K!$ as all stones $i \gt K$ will have one choice.

If $K \gt N$, then first stone paint will have $K$, second $K - 1$, ...., $N$-th stone will have $K-N+1$ choices. \
So the answer will be $K\times (K-1) \times \ldots \times (K-N+1) = \frac{K!}{(K-N)!}$

pages.title: MCQ - Paths Combinations
pages.content:
We make exactly $2N - 2$ moves, $N - 1$ are "right" moves and the other $N - 1$ are "down" moves. \
We want to align these moves such that there are exactly $K$ "turn" cells, meaning - we reach the cell with a move different than we leave the cell.

If we fix the first move to "right", in how many combinations can we reach the last cell.

1. $$
^{N - 2}C_{\lfloor\frac{K}{2}\rfloor} \cdot ^{N - 2}C_{\lfloor\frac{K - 1}{2}\rfloor}
$$

2. $$
^{N - 1}C_{\lfloor\frac{K}{2}\rfloor} \cdot ^{N - 1}C_{\lfloor\frac{K - 1}{2}\rfloor}
$$

3. $$
^{N}C_{\lfloor\frac{K}{2}\rfloor} \cdot ^{N}C_{\lfloor\frac{K - 1}{2}\rfloor}
$$

4. None of these

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: MCQ - Paths Combinations focuses on a specific combinatorics technique. Identify the counting model before implementing it.

pages.title: Concept - Path Counting Formula
pages.content:
Now if we make the the first move "down", we will have the same scenario as the previous one but rotated. 

So in this case, the answer will still be  
$$
^{N - 2}C_{\lfloor\frac{K}{2}\rfloor} \cdot ^{N - 2}C_{\lfloor\frac{K - 1}{2}\rfloor}
$$

practiceProblems.title: Permutation Subsequence
practiceProblems.description: Given an array and a target L, count the number of subsequences of length L whose values are exactly 1,2,...,L in some order.
practiceProblems.problemStatement: For a valid permutation subsequence, choose exactly one occurrence of each value from 1 through L. Since the values must all be distinct, the number of choices is the product of the frequencies of 1,2,...,L. Compute this product modulo 10^9+7.
constraints: The sum of N over all test cases <= 10^5
practiceProblems.inputFormat: The first line contains T. Each test case contains N L followed by the N array values.
practiceProblems.outputFormat: For each test case, print the number of valid permutation subsequences modulo 10^9+7.

sampleTestCases.explanation: The second test case has frequencies f1=3 and f2=3, so the answer is 9.

boilerPlates.Python3: # Solve the combinatorics problem using the specification above.\n

practiceProblems.title: Distance Coloring
practiceProblems.description: There are N stones in a row and K available colors. Stones whose positions differ by less than K must have different colors. Count the valid colorings modulo 10^9+7.
practiceProblems.problemStatement: The first K stones must all receive different colors. After that, stone i can only use the color of stone i-K, so every later stone has exactly one forced choice. Therefore the answer is K! when K <= N, and K*(K-1)*...*(K-N+1) when K > N.
practiceProblems.inputFormat: The first line contains T. Each following line contains N K.
practiceProblems.outputFormat: For each test case, print the number of valid colorings modulo 10^9+7.

sampleTestCases.explanation: The result is the falling factorial P(K,min(N,K)).

boilerPlates.Python3: # Solve the combinatorics problem using the specification above.\n

practiceProblems.title: Robot Movings
practiceProblems.description: A robot moves from the top-left corner of an N by N grid to the bottom-right corner using exactly N-1 right moves and N-1 down moves. Count paths having exactly K turns, assuming the first move is right.
practiceProblems.problemStatement: A turn occurs when the direction changes between consecutive moves. With the first move fixed as right, the number of paths with exactly K turns is C(N-2, floor(K/2)) * C(N-2, floor((K-1)/2)). Return the result modulo 10^9+7. If either binomial coefficient is invalid, the answer is 0.
practiceProblems.inputFormat: The first line contains T. Each following line contains N K.
practiceProblems.outputFormat: For each test case, print the number of valid paths modulo 10^9+7.

sampleTestCases.explanation: The formula follows from choosing the lengths of alternating horizontal and vertical runs.

boilerPlates.Python3: # Solve the combinatorics problem using the specification above.\n

practiceProblems.title: Marbles
practiceProblems.description: Hänschen chooses n marbles from k colors. Marbles of the same color are indistinguishable, order does not matter, and at least one marble of every color must be chosen. Count the possible selections.
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Give each of the k colors one marble first. The remaining n-k marbles can be distributed among k colors in C(n-1,k-1) ways. Print the exact result; the original problem guarantees it fits in signed 64-bit.
practiceProblems.inputFormat: The first line contains T. Each following line contains n k.
practiceProblems.outputFormat: For each test case, print C(n-1,k-1).

sampleTestCases.explanation: At least one marble per color reduces the problem to distributing the remaining n-k marbles.

boilerPlates.Python3: # Solve the combinatorics problem using the specification above.\n
